extracted.intended_audience: UIC Class VI permit applicants, project developers, state/tribal/federal UIC program regulators, and other stakeholders involved in geologic CO2 sequestration projects
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance and evaluative criteria for review, permitting, monitoring, and oversight of UIC Class VI geologic CO2 sequestration wells, including complementary GHGRP MRV reporting and environmental justice/public participation expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major components of a UIC Class VI permit
rubrics_metrics.description: Major components included in UIC Class VI permits are site characterization, area of review, corrective action, well construction and operation, testing and monitoring, financial responsibility, post-injection site care, well plugging, emergency and remedial response, and site closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These components are required under the UIC regulations (40 CFR parts 144-147) and form the basis of permitting decisions and permit conditions for Class VI geologic sequestration wells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of Underground Sources of Drinking Water (USDWs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permits must ensure the injection of CO2 does not endanger USDWs by preventing migration of injected CO2 or formation fluids out of the authorized injection zone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UIC program evaluates whether an application includes required information and supports a risk-based determination that USDWs will not be endangered; monitoring, permit conditions, and enforcement are tools to ensure protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multidisciplinary technical completeness and accuracy of permit applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Review entails a multidisciplinary evaluation to determine whether the application includes required information, is technically accurate, and supports a determination that USDWs will not be endangered by the proposed injection activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers include geologists, engineers, and physical scientists; applicants should submit complete, technically robust applications to avoid delays (e.g., respond timely to NODs/RAIs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Class VI-specific technical and monitoring requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Class VI wells have additional protective requirements tailored to large-scale geologic sequestration: more extensive geologic testing, detailed computational modeling of the project area and periodic re-evaluations, detailed requirements for monitoring and tracking the CO2 plume and pressure, unique financial responsibility requirements, and extended post-injection monitoring and site care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These requirements address risks unique to CO2 injection (large volumes, buoyancy, impurities, corrosivity, mobility) and are intended to ensure long-term containment and USDW protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency and Remedial Response Plan and response triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Class VI permits must include an Emergency and Remedial Response Plan; if monitoring indicates leakage of injected CO2 from the injection zone, this may trigger responses such as halting injection and implementation of remedial measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting authority may prescribe additional permit requirements or take enforcement actions if permit conditions are violated; permittees must be prepared to implement the plan when monitoring or inspections indicate problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced seismicity risk identification and management
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must identify, monitor, and reduce risks associated with induced seismicity through permit and program requirements such as site characterization and monitoring, and must demonstrate induced seismic activity will not endanger USDWs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategies are site-specific and may include supplemental seismic monitoring, altering operational parameters (rates/pressures), permit modification, partial plug back, controlled restart, suspending or revoking injection authorization, or shutting in a well. EPA may require seismic monitoring as a permit condition or deny permits with unacceptable seismic risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Site characterization requirements (including faults of concern and confining zone evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Site characterization must evaluate geologic and seismic data to identify faults of concern and ensure the confining zone is appropriate (e.g., free of faults of concern) and support safe injection operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If data indicate a substantial likelihood of seismic activity or other site-specific risks, EPA may require further analyses, additional monitoring, or planned operational changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational limits to reduce seismic and migration risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Operating requirements, such as ensuring injection pressure in the injection zone is below the fracture pressure, help reduce risks including injection-induced seismicity and unwanted fluid migration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits should include operational constraints and monitoring to ensure pressures and rates remain within safe bounds; regions may set conditions to stop or reduce injection if seismicity is detected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of CO2 retention as technical basis for oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory oversight is built upon proven mechanisms by which CO2 is retained: (1) structural and stratigraphic trapping, (2) residual CO2 trapping, (3) solubility trapping, (4) mineral trapping, and (5) preferential adsorption trapping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding and documenting which trapping mechanisms apply at a site informs monitoring design, modeling, long-term security assessments, and permit conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: GHGRP subpart RR reporting requirements for geologic sequestration
rubrics_metrics.description: GHGRP subpart RR requires reporting of the mass of CO2 received for injection, development and implementation of an EPA-approved MRV plan, reporting the mass of CO2 sequestered using a mass balance approach, and reporting annual monitoring activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subpart RR complements UIC monitoring/testing requirements (see 40 CFR 146.90-91) and applies to wells/groups that inject CO2 for long-term containment; reported non-confidential data are made public annually.

rubrics_metrics.name: MRV plan required components
rubrics_metrics.description: An MRV (monitoring, reporting, and verification) plan must include: (1) delineation of monitoring areas based on the CO2 plume location; (2) identification and evaluation of potential surface leakage pathways and an assessment of the likelihood, magnitude, and timing of surface leakage; (3) a strategy for detecting and quantifying any surface leakage of CO2 if leakage occurs; (4) an approach for establishing expected baselines for monitoring CO2 surface leakage; and (5) a summary of considerations made to calculate site-specific variables for the mass balance equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MRV plan is a primary complement to UIC subsurface monitoring and is often required to be EPA-approved as part of GHGRP subpart RR reporting obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: GHGRP subpart VV (EOR) requirements including EOR OMP
rubrics_metrics.description: GHGRP subpart VV applies to geologic sequestration associated with EOR using ISO 27916 and requires facilities to include in their annual report a copy of their EOR Operations Management Plan (EOR OMP) that: describes the EOR complex and engineered system; establishes that the EOR complex is adequate to provide safe, long-term containment of CO2; and includes site-specific information such as geologic characterization, description of facilities, all wells and engineered features, and operations history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilities that report under subpart RR must not also report under subpart VV; subpart VV is modeled largely after the ISO standard CSA/ANSI ISO 27916:2019.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class II vs Class VI applicability and transition criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Class II EOR injection wells are regulated to prevent endangerment to USDWs, but operators must obtain a Class VI permit when there is an increased risk to USDWs from changes in operations; the permitting authority (or operator) must assess factors specified in 40 CFR 144.19(b) including increase in reservoir pressure within the injection zone, increase in CO2 injection rates, and suitability of the Class II Area of Review delineation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an operator fails to notify the permitting authority when increased risk warrants transition to Class VI, they may be subject to enforcement and cessation of injection; permitting authorities also can require transition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathways by which injected fluids can endanger USDWs
rubrics_metrics.description: UIC regulations address major pathways for migration into USDWs: along the injection well bore, via improperly completed or plugged wells nearby, direct injection into a USDW, faults or fractures in confining strata, or lateral displacement into hydraulically connected USDWs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit applications and reviews must consider and address these pathways through AoR delineation, well construction standards, monitoring, corrective action plans, and other permit conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspections, monitoring report review, and enforcement to ensure compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The UIC program uses inspections, evaluation of periodic monitoring reports, discussions with operators, and, when necessary, administrative or judicial enforcement to address noncompliance and return wells to compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs may identify specific corrective actions for operators and may assist operators in returning wells to compliance; inspections verify compliance but are one of multiple oversight tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequestration leakage quantification and public reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Any leakage of CO2 at a sequestration facility must be quantified and reported under GHGRP subpart RR or subpart VV, and the reported data are made publicly available on the EPA's website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical data show reported leakage/emissions have been a small fraction of total sequestered amounts; reporting allows transparency and tracking of facility performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental justice (EJ) review and public participation expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants and EPA Regions should complete an EJ review using the EPA's EJScreen to identify disadvantaged communities within the Area of Review; if potential EJ impacts are identified, applicants/Regions should consider mitigation measures and enhanced, inclusive public participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended actions across five themes: identify communities with EJ concerns, enhance public involvement, conduct appropriately scoped EJ assessments, enhance transparency throughout permitting, and minimize adverse effects to USDWs and affected communities (e.g., early targeted outreach, mitigate language/technology barriers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting process management and target timeframes
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA aims to review complete Class VI applications and issue permits when appropriate within approximately 24 months; internal guidelines require Regions to classify applications received after Dec 12, 2023, as major new wells and develop project decision schedules with target timeframes for public comment periods and responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeframes depend on project complexity and application completeness; applicants should submit complete applications and respond timely to Requests for Additional Information (RAIs) or Notices of Deficiency (NODs) to avoid extending review time.

rubrics_metrics.name: State/tribal primacy application process for Class VI programs
rubrics_metrics.description: States may apply to EPA for primacy to administer Class VI programs; the primacy application process has four phases: (1) pre-application activities, (2) completeness review and determination, (3) application evaluation, and (4) rulemaking and codification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achieving primacy can shift permit reviews from EPA to the state/tribe, leveraging local expertise and potentially reducing EPA's application workload; EPA provides training, guidance, and IIJA grant support to build capacity for primacy.
